questiontext.text:
Goal

At an event entrance, a gate printer prints a ticket for each visitor. The spacing and line breaks on the tickets are wrong. Write welcome so that every ticket prints correctly on its own line.

Read
  • fmt.Println. Find the import line for this package. Read the first two sentences under Println. What separates the operands? What comes after the last one?
  • fmt.Print. Read the second sentence. When does this function add a space? Do the operands in this task meet that condition?
  • fmt.Printf. Read the first sentence. What argument does this function require that the other two do not?
Coming from Java

In Java, you might build one string with + before printing it. In Go, + can join two strings but cannot join a string and an int. That expression does not compile.

System.out.println("Ticket " + ticket + " for " + name);
Banned: Printf
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Work out what each permitted function prints for the four operands. Compare each result with the first visible test.
  • The hidden test prints two tickets in a row. Which function ends its output so that the next ticket starts on a new line?

expected.text: Ticket 7 for Ada Ticket 8 for Linus

questiontext.text:
Goal

An evidence room records each item as staff book it into storage. Its program should print one line per item, but it does not compile. Make it compile without changing that line.

Read
  • Import declarations. Find the paragraph after the table. Which clause applies to the starter file?
  • Variable declarations. Read the last sentence. Which variables does it restrict? Where does the restriction apply?
Coming from Java

In Java, an unused import and an unused local variable produce IDE warnings. The program still compiles, so a Java developer might leave them for later.

import java.util.List;   // unused, still builds

String note;             // unused, still builds
Banned: _
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Search the Import declarations section for the word "illegal".
  • Compare each declaration with both clauses of the implementation restriction in the Variable declarations section.

expected.text: Booked 1 of knife on shelf B4
Booked 3 of phones on shelf B4
Booked 0 of bag of coins on shelf C2

questiontext.text:
Goal

A roadside signpost tells drivers how far remains and gives advice for the journey. Write signpost to print the distance and the advice on separate lines. Say Keep driving for 10 miles or more, Nearly there below that, and You have arrived at 0 miles.

Read
  • If statements. Find the IfStmt line. Which parts are optional? What must follow the condition? In the second example, what can follow else? Where does else appear relative to the closing brace?
  • Comparison operators. Read the first sentence and the table. Which operators return a value that an if statement can use as its condition?
Coming from Java

In Java, you can put parentheses around the condition and omit braces for a one-line body. Go's grammar does not require those parentheses, and gofmt removes them. Go always requires the braces.

if (miles == 0) System.out.println("You have arrived");
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Start with the structure of the first example under the IfStmt line.
  • Three cases require two decisions. Check the IfStmt line. What can follow else?

expected.text: 0 miles to go You have arrived
